The Radiated shanny (Ulvaria subbifurcata) is a small benthic fish endemic to the northwestern Atlantic, whose life-history traits reflect the cool, productive waters it inhabits. Newly hatched larvae emerge from the egg during a developmental period that varies with thermal conditions; when incubation occurs at a mean temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the embryo completes development to hatch in approximately 35 days [ab = approximately 35 days]. This extended embryonic phase is typical of stichaeid fishes that deposit demersal eggs in cold, shallow inshore habitats. The prolarvae that emerge at hatching are endotrophic, subsisting entirely on their yolk reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding. Upon yolk-sac resorption, the free-swimming larvae must locate suitable planktonic prey to sustain growth, a critical transition that strongly influences first-year survival. The timing of this pelagic larval phase aligns with the spring bloom of copepod nauplii, a key resource pulse in Newfoundland fjords where this species is commonly collected.

As the pelagic larva grows and undergoes metamorphosis, it gradually shifts from a planktonic existence to a demersal, benthic juvenile lifestyle. The standard length at which individuals attain sexual maturity is 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 3.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.9 grams]. This length-based threshold is reached after a period of rapid juvenile growth, during which the fish must acquire sufficient somatic mass to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation and gametogenesis onset. At the onset of reproduction for the radiated shanny, females produce a single clutch of demersal eggs per spawning season [F_R_i = single clutch of demersal eggs per spawning season]. The maximum annual reproductive output, observed under favorable environmental conditions at a stable water temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C], is estimated at approximately 1512 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1512 eggs per year], a high fecundity for a fish of this body size.

The ultimate standard length achieved by adult radiated shanny is 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], representing the asymptotic size at which somatic growth effectively ceases. Correspondingly, this length yields a predicted ultimate wet weight of approximately 35.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 35.2 grams] for a fully grown individual, based on the length-weight relationship established for this species. This maximum body size is modest relative to other stichaeid fishes, such as the Arctic shanny (Stichaeus punctatus), which can exceed 25 cm in standard length. The relatively small adult body size of Ulvaria subbifurcata is consistent with its cryptic, rock-crevice-dwelling habit and its reliance on small benthic invertebrates, primarily amphipods and polychaetes, as prey. The cessation of somatic growth in late adulthood presumably reflects the reallocation of available resources toward reproductive effort and the physiological limitations of maintaining somatic tissues in an aging individual.

The lifespan of the radiated shanny, recorded from otolith-based ageing studies, reaches a maximum of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under natural conditions at a mean ambient water temperature of 6.4 °C [T = 6.4 °C]. This longevity is notably high for a relatively small-bodied teleost and suggests a slow-paced life-history strategy, characterized by late maturation, iteroparous spawning, and low natural mortality among adults. The extended lifespan may be an adaptation to the variable and seasonally harsh conditions of the northwestern Atlantic shelf, where favourable recruitment years are sporadic, and adult survival buffers the population against prolonged periods of poor larval or juvenile survival. The onset of exogenous feeding at approximately 35 days [ab = approximately 35 days] represents only a brief fraction of the total lifespan, emphasizing the extended juvenile and adult phases that dominate the speci at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]es' life cycle.

The wet weight at birth for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is extremely low, at only 0.0019 grams [Wwb = 0.0019 grams], a value that derives from the egg's small diameter of roughly 1.55 mm. This minuscule initial mass places the radiated shanny among the smallest-born of the Stichaeidae, and it imposes intense selective pressure on the larva to locate and consume adequate planktonic prey within the first few days of exogenous feeding, before its endogenous yolk reserves are fully depleted. The period of yolk-sac larval life, during which the larva is essentially a non-feeding alevin dependent on lecithotrophic nutrition, is therefore a critical bottleneck in the early life history. Successful transition to exogenous feeding, marked by mouth opening and first prey capture, sets the trajectory for juvenile growth and, ultimately, for the attainment of the 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm] standard length at which sexual maturation begins.
